procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 13, 14, 1967 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 380 of 1966, and delivered a judgment and order on December 13 and 14, 1967. The outcome of the appeal is not explicitly stated, but it can be inferred that the High Court upheld the conviction of the appellant (Accused No. 4) to some extent, as he is appealing that decision to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal only to Accused No. 4. The Supreme Court initially declined special leave against the conviction of the other three co-accused, making their convictions final. The Supreme Court, deviating from its usual practice under Article 136 of the Constitution, examined the evidence because it was represented that the evidence did not support the High Court's conclusion and that grave injustice had been caused.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction for the charges under s. 302 read with s. 109 I.P.C. and of conspiracy is upheld. The conviction for the charge under s. 302 read with s. 34 is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence established the appellant's complicity in the murder to support the charges under Section 302 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and for conspiracy.

facts.fact: There were constant disputes and strained relations between the appellant (accused no. 4) and the deceased over a right of passage and water, which established animus (motive).
The day before the murder, the appellant exhorted his companions to kill the deceased.
On the day of the murder, the appellant threatened to kill the deceased.
A witness, Jaitunbi (P.W. 5), testified that on the night of the murder, the appellant told his nephew to move from a cot because a dead body was going to be placed there.
Another witness, Laxmibai (P.W. 7), saw the appellant with two other persons following the deceased just 15-20 minutes before the murder occurred.

law.law_text: Section 109 of the IPC (abetment) can be applied even if the abettor is not present when the crime is committed, as long as they instigated the offence or engaged in a conspiracy to commit it.

Criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B is an agreement between two or more people to do an illegal act. Since conspiracies are hatched in secret, they can be proven by circumstantial evidence, including surrounding circumstances and the antecedent and subsequent conduct of the accused.

application.application_text: The Court found that the evidence of the long-standing disputes, combined with the appellant's open threats and exhortations to kill the deceased, fully established both his animus and his role in instigating the murder.

The testimony that the appellant was preparing for a dead body and was seen following the victim shortly before the attack was considered strong circumstantial evidence supporting the charge of a pre-planned criminal conspiracy.

The Court concluded that this collective evidence was sufficient to prove the appellant's involvement, noting that proof of conspiracy is often inferential but must be founded on solid facts, which it found to be present in this case.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the evidence clearly established the appellant's complicity in the murder. The combination of motive (strained relations), direct instigation (threats and exhortations to kill), and circumstantial evidence linking him to the crime immediately before it happened was sufficient to fully support the convictions for abetment of murder under Section 302 read with Section 109 IPC and for criminal conspiracy.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt the appellant's presence at or near the spot of the murder to sustain a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

facts: A witness, Jaitunbi (P.W. 5), testified that on the night of the murder, the appellant told his nephew to move from a cot because a dead body was to be kept there.
Another witness, Laxmibai (P.W. 7), testified that the appellant, along with two other persons, followed the deceased about 20 minutes before the murder was reported.
law: To sustain a conviction, the prosecution must prove the accused's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt."
A finding that something is "highly probable" does not meet the standard of proof required for a criminal conviction.
application: The Supreme Court considered the evidence and found it made the appellant's presence at or near the scene of the murder "highly probable."
However, the Court determined that this evidence was not sufficient to prove his presence "beyond a reasonable doubt."
The Court reasoned that it was possible that after following the deceased, the appellant stayed away while the other co-accused were the only ones who actually took part in the murder.
This possibility created a reasonable doubt regarding the appellant's presence at the exact time and place of the crime.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt and set aside his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the IPC, because the evidence did not establish his presence at or near the spot of the murder beyond a reasonable doubt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence established the appellant's complicity in the murder to support the charges under Section 302 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and for conspiracy.
appellant_arguments: The evidence presented did not support the High Court's conclusion and was insufficient to establish complicity in the murder or involvement in a conspiracy.
respondent_arguments: The evidence, particularly the testimony of Jaitunbi (P.W. 5) that the appellant told his nephew to clear a cot for a dead body, and Laxmibai (P.W. 7) that the appellant was seen following the deceased with others just before the murder, was sufficient to prove a pre-hatched plan and the appellant's complicity.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt the appellant's presence at or near the spot of the murder to sustain a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
appellant_arguments: The evidence was not enough to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant was present at the spot when the murder was actually committed.
It is possible that after following the deceased, the appellant stayed away and only the other co-accused took part in the actual murder.
respondent_arguments: The evidence that the appellant followed the deceased just before the murder made it highly probable that he was present with the other co-accused at the time of the murder.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 34 embodies the principle of joint liability in the doing of a criminal act, the essence of which is the existence of a common intention. Participation in the commission of the offence in furtherance of the common intention is required for its application, and the accused's presence at or near the spot of the crime must be established beyond a reasonable doubt.
obiter: It was highly probable that at the time of the actual murder the appellant was either present with the other three co-accused or was somewhere nearby.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The evidence clearly established the appellant's complicity in the murder, and the charges under s. 302 read with s. 109 I.P.C. and of conspiracy were fully supported by the evidence. However, regarding the charge under s. 302 read with s. 34, while it was highly probable that the appellant was present with the other co-accused or nearby at the time of the actual murder, the evidence did not establish his presence at or near the spot beyond a reasonable doubt, entitling him to the benefit of doubt on that specific charge.
legal_tests_applied: Section 34 embodies the principle of joint liability in the doing of a criminal act, the essence of that liability being the existence of a common intention. Participation in the commission of the offence in furtherance of the common intention invites its application.
For a conspiracy charge, an inference can be drawn from the circumstances that a plan was hatched out prior to the incident and that the criminal act was done in pursuance of that pre-planning.
why_appellant_lost: The Court considered the appellant's case in the background of the fact that the conviction of the other three co-accused had become final.
The High Court's inference of a pre-hatched plan was found to be reasonable, based on the circumstance that all four accused followed the deceased just before the murder.

The High Court's decision to believe the evidence of witnesses, who were described as independent, was upheld. This included the key evidence that the appellant was seen following the deceased just before the murder with two or three other persons.
why_respondent_won: The case against the appellant was considered in the context of the final conviction of the other three co-accused, which strengthened the prosecution's case.

The court accepted the High Court's reasoning that an inference of a pre-planned conspiracy could be reasonably drawn from the established circumstances, particularly the act of the accused following the deceased together.

The High Court's reliance on witness testimony, especially the evidence that the appellant was seen following the deceased just before the murder, was deemed sufficient to uphold the conviction for conspiracy and abetment.
policy_considerations: The Court must give the accused the benefit of doubt when the evidence does not establish a fact beyond a reasonable doubt, as was the case with the appellant's actual presence at the spot of the murder.
The Supreme Court may examine the evidence in an appeal by special leave, contrary to its usual practice, to ensure justice is served.
